connector: Three chapters, and one question asked three times: whom do you trust, and what does trusting cost? Today you test your theme sentence on a character you haven’t used yet. If it holds, bring the page that proves it. If it doesn’t, make it wider.

a.raw: caspian spoke sadly of nikabrik and said he had gone sour inside from long suffering and hateing
a.fixed: Caspian spoke sadly of Nikabrik and said, “He had gone sour inside from long suffering and hating.”
a.why: Capitals on Caspian, Nikabrik and He; a comma before the quotation; hating drops the silent e before -ing; the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.

b.raw: wraiths and wreckage gasped trumpkin in the ghost of a voice
b.fixed: “Wraiths and wreckage!” gasped Trumpkin in the ghost of a voice.
b.why: Lewis’s own sentence. Capitals on Wraiths and Trumpkin; the exclamation point goes inside the quotation marks; a period ends the sentence.

vocab: A very steep cliff or drop.
A rough camp without proper shelter.
Able to feel and sense things; aware.
Betraying your own king or country.
notes.wordParts: Latin bases: rupt = break, duct and duce = lead, form = shape: interrupt, conduct, introduce, transform.
notes.grammar: Commas in dates and places: a comma between the day and the year (June 12, 1941), between a town and its county or country (Dover, Kent), and another after them if the sentence goes on. Narnia has no calendar, so practice dates are made up. Editing day.
notes.spelling: Greek and Latin parts you know: port (carry), spect (look), script and scribe (write), rupt (break), tele (far). Spell the part the same way every time: inter + rupt + ion.

grammar.label: Nell · check every date and place

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Nell. Three chapters, one question asked three times: whom do you trust, and what does it cost? Today’s question: does your theme sentence hold for everyone?
transcripts.read: Say your theme sentence out loud. Then try it on someone you haven’t used yet: Susan, Trumpkin, Nikabrik, Caspian. If it fits, find the page. If it doesn’t, change the sentence. Never leave the character out to protect it.
transcripts.grammar: Editing day. Read each date and place. Is there a comma between the day and the year? Between the town and the bigger place? And if the sentence keeps going, is there a comma after? Fix each one and say what it separates.

steps: Read the tip and the lenses.
Tap the lens you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you read. Your note boxes are on the Reading tab.
Tap each yellow part of the first sentence to see why it is correct.
Pick Sentence A or Sentence B.
Type it the right way in the box, then tap Check My Work.
Read the lines from the poem.
Think about which character keeps a steady head.
Write your thinking in the box.
Play the quick match.
Pick one base and think how you’d explain it.
Read the word list.
Pick one option from the choice board.
Write it in the box, starting with the letter you chose.
Read each line.
Tap every line with a comma problem.
In the box, fix one and say what each comma separates.
Read the words.
Tap only the ones that are wrong.
In the box, fix one and name its root and prefix.
Look back at Chapters 10 to 12.
Fill in the note boxes: your theme sentence and a new character to test it on.
Think about the three questions.
Then do the Seven Pillars Watch at the end of this tab.
Pick Explorer or Scholar.
Answer all three questions in full sentences.
Use a detail from the book in every answer. The hint under each question helps.
Last, write one or two sentences about your reading lens.
State a theme in one sentence.
Give two examples from Chapters 10–12 and explain how each one shows it.
